title: "Set 11 — hierarchical clustering"

Data: [`customers.csv`](../materials/customers.csv). Take a random sample of 300
rows — a full dendrogram of 6 000 is unreadable, and that is itself part of the
lesson:

```r
set.seed(11)
s <- customers[sample(nrow(customers), 300), ]
```

The Blackboard test checks your numbers against this sample.

## 1 · Four linkages, four trees

Build the distance matrix on scaled columns, then cluster with `complete`,
`average`, `single` and `ward.D2`. Plot the four dendrograms.

One of them produces a long thin tree with points joining one at a time. Name
it, and explain the mechanism that causes it.

## 2 · Cut, and compare

Cut the Ward tree at `k = 4` with `cutree`. Cross-tabulate against k-means on
the same 300 scaled rows: `set.seed(11)`, then `kmeans(scale(s[, 2:7]), 4,
nstart = 25)`.

How many customers do the two methods place together? Where they disagree, is it
a few points on a boundary or an entire segment split differently?

## 3 · The height axis means something

On the Ward dendrogram, find the two largest jumps in merge height.

What would cutting at each of them give you, and which cut would you defend?
Why is a large jump evidence, and what is the argument it is *not* proof?

## 4 · When the tree is the deliverable [In class]{.badge-class}

[We discuss this one in lecture 13, on 13 Nov — bring your answer.]{.muted}

Hierarchical clustering gives you a nested structure that k-means cannot.

Describe one business question where the *nesting* is the answer — where
knowing that segment A splits into A1 and A2 changes a decision — and one where
the flat partition is all anybody needs.

## Check yourself on Blackboard

Open the test **Set 11** on Blackboard, enter your numbers, and read the feedback as soon as you submit. Not graded; as many attempts as you like.
